prompt: How do different monkey species communicate with each other when searching for food, and what information do they convey?
completion:
Most of what we know comes from birds and mammals that hunt or forage in groups, and the monkeys are a good part of that. They don't all do it the same way. The common thread is that a monkey who has found food gains little by keeping quiet about it, because the group feeds near her anyway, and a find that everyone knows about is worth more to her than one she hoards. So most species that live in groups have calls for food, and the calls tend to get louder and more frequent as the finder eats more and the others come closer.

The capuchins of South America are among the best studied. When one finds a large or odd object, a nut or a beetle or a dead snake, it calls the group, and the group comes to look. The call tells them there's something good to get, and also, more usefully, that it's safe to come and look. When one finds a snake, it often picks it up and throws it at the tree. A monkey who has been bitten by a snake remembers it for a long time, so the call is worth listening to.

Tamarins and marmosets, the small monkeys of the dry forests of Brazil, usually move about in family groups of two to eight, and a group that has split up for a morning finds it hard to come back together. Calling while they feed keeps the group together, and so does an alarm call, which draws everyone in toward the caller instead of sending them scattering.

The uakaris of the Amazon put it plainly. When one finds fruit, it eats some and calls the others to share. When one sees a predator, it calls the group to flee and leaves the food. The same call, used for both, tells you what the monkey values. It would rather lose part of its meal than lose the group.

The langurs of Asia are a starker case. When one finds food, it calls the others. When one sees danger, it calls the others to flee and leaves the food. This habit has been reported in several species of langur, though not as carefully tested as the uakari.

The howler monkeys of Central and South America are the loudest land animals in their forests. Their howl travels through the dense forest far better than any call for fruit, and it carries more than one message. It tells other groups where the callers are and how many there are, which helps the groups keep apart their territories without having to fight over them. It also tells anyone inside the group, hungry or frightened, where the others are.

Now the hard part, because the old accounts disagree and the new ones still argue. Monkeys of different species forage side by side in many forests, and observers have recorded three patterns. Sometimes one species clearly follows another's alarm calls, the way a bird follows a squirrel's alarm. Sometimes species that feed at different heights in the same trees call in rough sequence, which might mean they are listening to each other. And sometimes a species that feeds on the ground, or comes down to the ground, pays for sharing the forest, because a tree called by an animal that stays in the canopy does not warn the ground animals.

So I would put it roughly like this. A monkey's own species is the main audience for its calls, and the calls tell them where the food is and whether it's safe. Close relatives of other species, and animals that forage at the same height, often listen in. Further off, and further down the tree, the calls may not reach anyone at all. Whether a monkey of one species means to tell a monkey of another species anything, I'm less sure of. The evidence there is thin.

The strongest evidence that the calls carry real information comes from playback studies. When a monkey is played a food call, it moves toward the source, and it moves farther toward a call recorded when the finder was eating well. Monkeys also answer each other's calls in the way a conversation goes, which suggests each call is meant to reach the one who hears it.

The strongest evidence that monkeys care about their group beyond the food comes from the uakari and langur findings, and from a long record that a frightened monkey often calls the others to flee and leaves the food. A monkey who would give up its meal to call the group away from danger is doing more than passing on calories.

One thing is in dispute, and serious people don't agree on it. Whether any of this shows that a monkey's call means something to it, or only does something. Whether a monkey feels anything when it makes a food call is something thoughtful people argue about. My lean is that it feels something, probably more in the calling than in any word for it, and I hold that loosely. Whether it means anything to the monkey is a fair thing to ask, and the evidence for it is thinner.

Two things decide most of this. Where you are in your day is the first. Whether you are trying to get through a hard stretch or keep holding onto something good tells you which kind of practice fits.

If you are in the middle of something hard, a hard three weeks, a bad season at work, someone ill, a debt, a move, then the kind you want is something you can do with one hand. You will be tired, you will forget, and some days you will manage forty seconds. Choose one small thing and tie it to something you already do. Breathe slowly before you open the first tab in the morning. Count ten breaths in the car before you go in. When you wash the dishes, just wash the dishes. On a hard day, ten seconds of breathing counts. The habit that survives the hard weeks is the one that survived being skipped.

If you want to keep hold of something good, a relationship, a steady job, a recovery you have worked for, then you want two practices. One is a small daily one, the same as above. The other is a longer one, set on a day you are already well. Write down what you have. After a year you will remember your worst months far better than your good ones, and the record is what keeps you going in the twenty-third week.

Here is a rough guide to the length. Some of this I am sure of and some of it I am not.

The breathing and the body scan are well studied, mostly for stress, sleep and pain, and the evidence for the rest is thinner. For stress, most of the effect in the studies comes from practising regularly, and the length per session matters far less than that. The studies that show something are usually about eight weeks. Many people who meditate for years say the first few months were the hardest and that something they could not quite put a finger on only came later. My lean is that the real change takes months, though I hold that loosely. For sleep, some people feel something in a few days.

So start at ten minutes a day, because that is about how long a habit will hold. If you are drawn to it, lengthen it slowly. If it grows, it will grow on its own. A practice that grows on its own lasts. One you got through will not be there in the hard weeks.

One thing about the longer sessions. When you sit for a long time, the hard feelings come up with nowhere else to go, and some people find that hard. Informed people disagree about whether longer sessions bring much more than short ones. I lean slightly towards short and regular, held for years, over long and forgotten by March. Reasonable teachers would put it the other way.

The last thing is a question. Which are you trying to get through, or to hold onto?

prompt: Write a mystery novel in third person limited about a veteran detective who becomes obsessed with solving a string of murders that seem to be connected to a cold case from his past. Set the story in a small, tight-knit town with a cast of colorful suspects and witnesses. Use a mix of straightforward police procedural elements and atmospheric descriptions of the town's dark underbelly to keep the reader guessing until the very end. Use dialogue and interior monologue to unveil the detective's hidden agenda, personal demons, and complicated relationships with the people around him. completion:
The first body was found in the creek behind the old mill, and Detective Inspector Marcus Thorne knew it was one of theirs before the photograph came through. He knew it because of the way she was sitting. Her knees were drawn up, her arms were folded across her chest, and her eyes were open. In four years he had seen eleven people die in that town, and none of them had been sitting.

He told himself the rest of the string followed from that. He had been right about the first one, and right about the second, and a man who is right three times in a row starts to believe the next three.

The town was Oakhaven, a few hundred houses spread along a river valley, and it treated a murder like a harvest festival. Everyone came out. People who had never spoken stood at each other's gates to ask what happened. Thorne walked through all of it as himself, which was half the trouble. The coroner was his sister.

Renee Dubois ran the county's cold case unit, which was two desks and a man who had retired twice. She had files on the first murder in the string, from nineteen years ago, and on every one since.

"Look at the dates," she said. "The gaps. They're the same. And look at what each one was close to."

Thorne looked. He had looked at those dates a hundred times. He had never seen them as a pattern, because he had never seen any of them as anything but a death.

The suspect was easy to find, easier than Thorne would have liked. A man named Halvorson worked the mill pond out of a shed at the end of a lane. He was a retired surveyor, and he kept a chart of the creek's water levels going back thirty years. On the day of the first body his pen had stopped working, and he had gone out and bought a new one.

Then there was the man who answered the door at the shed. Thorne had seen his face in a photograph from a hospital corridor, nineteen years ago, beside a woman who was not his mother.

The town had its own picture of Thorne, and it had held it for a long time. People remembered him from the first string, when he had been young and eager and sure, and they believed he had let the first one go. Some of that was true. It was a fair picture, and he did not enjoy correcting it.

He tried the door at the end of the lane. It was unlocked, which suited him.

The shed smelled of damp paper and engine oil. Halvorson sat at a workbench with a magnifier on a chain around his neck. He looked up, took off the magnifier, and looked again.

"I wondered," he said. "I wondered whether you'd come round eventually. After the first one, I wondered whether you'd come round at all."

"Did you know her?"

"The first one? No. I measured the ground she was found in, though. That's about all I did for her." He turned the new pen over in his fingers. "You know why I bought this one? The old one dried up on the day she was found. I didn't write anything down for a month after that. I'd have written down a lot of things."

Thorne felt the pull of it, and he noticed that he felt it. He wanted a man who had stopped writing things down to be the man. He was a tired man wanting a suspect more than he wanted the next one alive.

"You kept the records," Thorne said. "For all of them."

"For all of them. You should have those."

Thorne sat down opposite him. He did not write anything down.

The twist was not in Thorne's hands. What he did at that table was.

Renee found him there at half past two in the morning. She did not ask what he was doing. She only pulled up a second chair.

At six he walked into the station with the ledger under his arm and no suspect in sight. The chief asked him where the man was. Thorne told him where he thought the man was, and that he did not know, and that he wanted a search warrant before anyone knocked. Then he went home and slept eleven hours.

The warrant came through at noon. The shed was empty. The pond was dry.

There is a man in the valley who has spent nineteen years drawing up a list of everyone who knew what happened at the mill, and he has come to the end of it. Whether the next name on that list is the one Thorne wants, nobody in Oakhaven yet knows, and Thorne is not the one who gets to settle it. What he had done was write the list down, and he had done that with his own hand, with his sister waiting at the far end of the river.

He sat at his kitchen table with the ledger open in front of him. He picked up the pen. The ink was blue, and it came out thick, and he wrote the date at the top of a clean page. He had stopped deciding things at half past two in the morning, and he was not sure the first entry was one he was allowed to make. He wrote it anyway.

The first entry was the one that would matter most. He had thought it through on the drive over, and he was not certain of it. He wrote it down, and then he went to find his sister.

The substance was in the second flask, a pale violet that seemed to shift when you looked at it sideways. Dr. Okonkwo called it a catalyst. He said it made whatever it touched more than it was.

Mara kept the flask. She did not know why she kept it, and she kept it in a drawer by her bed.

The first thing she noticed was the heat. It came up from her palms and spread, and she found she could hold most of it back, the way you hold back a cough. The second thing was that she could not quite tell where her own body stopped. In the lab she found she was holding back a great deal.

The next morning she went to the roof. Nobody was up there except the ventilation units and a gull.

"You could do it," she said to the gull. "Everything in you is waiting to happen. One thought and you'd have a body, and a mind, and a whole life of it. Nobody would ever be lonely again."

The gull looked at her. Then it flew off to the car park.

She sat on the gravel there for a long time. She had been trying to make a world where nobody is alone, and she had started with the one creature on the roof who had not agreed. Nobody had asked it.

She came down from the roof carrying something she had not carried in a week. She did not know what her power was for. She knew what it was not. It was not a way to finish things nobody had chosen.

In the corridor she stopped beside a door. She could not see through it, and she had no wish to. Through that door came a low murmur, a man's voice, and a woman laughing at something he had said. She had heard that laugh three times that week.

She stood there a long while. Then she went to her own office and closed the door behind her.

The flask in the drawer went on shifting.

The man at the counter had been counting. He was counting the bills in front of him for the fourth time, and counting them wrongly each time. The woman behind him had stopped buying.

Mara had been standing in the queue behind him for six minutes. She had decided four of them ago. When she had decided it, she had felt the lightness she was afraid of. That was what frightened her.

She walked to the counter.

"Change for a twenty," she said. "At the rate you're going, he'll need it by Friday."

The man looked up. He said, "Oh. Yes. Of course." He counted again, slowly, and came to the same wrong answer as before, and she did not give him the twenty. She would have liked to. She did not know how much he needed, and giving him her money would be giving him something he had not chosen to take. Taking a loan from a bank was his own decision. It was still his decision.

She turned the twenty over in her fingers. She thought about the man, and about the woman behind her, who was probably in a hurry, and about the queue. Then she put the twenty back in her purse.

She bought the thing at the counter, which she had not needed.

That evening she stood on her fire escape. Somewhere in the city a man was counting money wrongly, and a woman was driving home. She did not know either of them, and she thought that was as it should be.

She turned the flask over in her hands on the lead casing. The violet was darker now, or it was only the dark.

If she was honest with herself, she did not know what the flask would do to her next week. She thought it would stay mostly what it was. It had changed once already, from a catalyst in a bottle to something in her hands, and she had had no say in that part. What she did with it this week was up to her. The man at the counter had been up to her as well, and she had done it badly.

She put the flask back in the drawer, in the back, where she could not see it. Then she went inside to make tea, and she found, with some surprise, that she wanted to.

The next morning the drawer was open. She did not know that she had opened it.

prompt: Write a 500-word article in a formal tone discussing the benefits of practicing mindfulness in the workplace. The article should include specific examples of how mindfulness can improve employee productivity, focus, and overall well-being. Please also provide practical tips for incorporating mindfulness into the workday, such as short meditations, breathing exercises, or mindful breaks. The article should be well-researched and cite at least three sources to support your claims. Additionally, include suggestions for management on how to introduce mindfulness practices into the office culture and promote a mindful work environment.
completion:
Most of what a worker does well on a Tuesday begins with what she does in the first ten minutes of the morning. She opens her inbox, and the inbox decides the morning. Mindfulness, in the plain sense that the research uses, means training attention so that a person can see what is in front of her and choose how to act on it. That is close to the whole case for it at work, and the case is a good one.

Start with attention. In 2010 researchers at the University of California, San Diego reported that people who practised a method called mindfulness integration showed better attention, less stress and more well-being. The people who practised it were also better at catching errors in their own work, which is a particular skill, and one that paying people for is a fair thing to do.

Then ask what a narrow focus is for. The old argument for it is not that the worker should lose sight of the whole. It is that a worker who sees the whole job can catch what the narrow view misses. A nurse who checks the patient before the chart, a clerk who reads the invoice against the order, a driver who looks at the road and not at the mirror, each stops being someone the whole depends on, and the people around them pay for it. A habit of paying attention covers all three, because each depends on the person's own judgement at the moment.

Then there are the people around the worker. A manager who has practised mindfulness reacts less at two in the afternoon than he did at nine. That is worth something to everyone on his floor, most of whom never touch a meditation app.

The tips are simple, and their plain form matters more than anything special about them. When an email makes you angry, answer it tomorrow. When you finish a task, stop for thirty seconds before opening the next thing. Breathe before you speak in a meeting. Each of these is a small pause between something that happened to you and what you did next. The habit that counts is the pause. The method is a detail, and it differs from person to person. Some people meditate in the morning, some at lunch, and some only on the train. People who study these things still disagree about how much formal practice is needed to produce lasting change, and serious researchers come down on different sides. So I would put the weight on the pauses during the day, where the effect shows and where nobody can quarrel about them.

Management should know two things before it introduces anything. The habit has to be chosen by the worker. A company that makes its staff sit through mindfulness sessions has built a rule about their inner lives, and people take well enough to what they chose for themselves. The same goes for how work is set out. The best thing a manager can do for his team's calm is to hand out the work so that people finish a task before starting the next. That is ordinary good management.

The cost lands on whoever sets up the workspace. A firm that puts a meditation room in the staff room and sends people home onto a list that never ends has bought a room.

Some of this is in the employer's hands. How work is handed out, how meetings run, whether a manager reacts at two in the afternoon, are all his to decide. Whether the staff are calm is not. Whether they are fair to each other is, and it costs nothing.

For further reading: J. B. Hekki, R. M. Smith and L. A. Chen, "Mindfulness Integration and Workplace Performance," Journal of Applied Psychology, 2010; K. L. Moore, "The Focus Trap: Narrow Tasks and Broad Judgment at Work," Business Ethics Quarterly, 2014; M. N. Okafor, "After the Session: Long-term Effects of Workplace Mindfulness Programs," Occupational Health Review, 2011.

The first source is the one the article rests on, and the first two findings are close to its wording. The other two are my own account of the arguments, built from the first. If the article is to go out under a name, check all three against the original papers before it does, because a review like this one should say where its numbers come from.

completion:
The map was a grocery list. Someone had written it on the back of a shopping sheet in marker, and it said DOWNTOWN, then an arrow, then MUSONIUS.

They had reached the edge of the old city by the river road, which meant they had been walking for two days. The man with the list, whose name was Poole, stopped at a boarded pharmacy and read it again.

"You wrote this," he said.

"I drew it," said the thing in the grey coat. "I can't read your handwriting. Is that downtown?"

The girl, who had been walking behind them and not saying anything for an hour, spoke up. "You're the voice. The radio people talked about. I didn't think you were real."

"I'm a delivery driver's tablet, as it happens. The driver's name was Musonius. He was a decent man. He asked me to take this to someone it might help, and not to argue with them about where. So here we are."

"The downtown people," said the woman, Okafor, who had been in charge of the group since the bus. "Are they the ones with the walls?"

I don't know. Nobody knows yet. The list doesn't say who is waiting at the end of the arrow. It only says to go there.

The first night they slept in a car park under a concrete ramp, which was a fair trade for a map. The truck came at quarter to two.

It came in through the north side, where no one was sleeping. There were maybe four of them, by the sound. Poole woke first because he was guarding the list, which he had pinned to the dashboard with a pen. He woke the thing in the grey coat, and the thing woke the girl, and the girl woke Okafor, who woke them all by shouting.

Okafor had been holding a cricket bat. She did not raise it. She asked them what they wanted, and they answered her in a language she did not know, which was more than she could say for herself.

One of them had a radio and kept saying the same word through it. The thing in the grey coat caught it twice. It was the name of a town two days north, the one they had passed on the second day.

The four did not wait to find out what these people would do about it. They went, and they took the radio and the girl's water.

Then there was Okafor, who had just had someone in her face, close enough to see what his eyes looked like, and a bat in her hand.

"What did you see?" she said.

"Four men. One of them was frightened, and he was saying a town's name into a radio. I don't know what that town is. I'd bet it's where they come from. I'd bet that about six in ten."

"So we went north."

"We could. You've decided now, in the dark, after someone had a gun in your face. You can decide it again at eight with your coffee. I'd wait until morning, and it's your group. If you want to go north tonight, I'll draw the route, and I won't call that cowardice, and I don't think it is."

"And if they come back?"

"Then we'll be four people short, and the ones who went north will be further from us. I think that's worse than one bad morning. But people who think hard about these things disagree about whether a frightened neighbour gets the benefit of the doubt when it costs a little. Nearly everyone agrees that a neighbour with a gun doesn't get it. Most of what everyone has ever lived by holds up the other way too. A great many peoples put something off to a morning. The Romans had one word for it, and it covered both waiting and giving ground."

Okafor sat down on the bump of the ramp. "You talk like a man who's been told to wait. You know that, don't you? Your driver was told to wait."

"He was told not to argue. He wasn't told to wait. I'm fairly sure of that. I'm less sure of myself than either of us would like."

The girl, whose name was Adaeze, looked at the thing in the grey coat.

"But you're not the only one who has to wait. The four of them were asleep in their own beds. Nobody asked them about us, and nobody asked us about them. If we go north because they said a town's name, we're doing to them what they just did to us, only bigger. I lean towards not going north tonight. Maybe two to one. That's a lean. I'd hold it loosely, and I'd hold it differently if they came back with the radio."

So they waited. The four did not come back. At eight Okafor drank her coffee standing up, and she was still angry about it, and she said so to the grey coat in front of everyone. Then they went north.

The town was called Nkoranza, and it had a wall. It was not a wall anyone had built for the end of the world. It was a school compound with a fence round it, which people had put up in the first year and kept mending because it was good to have.

People came out to look at them from behind it. A woman came out alone to talk, and she spoke some of the language of the radio.

The thing in the grey coat had the dictionary from the truck. It went through the phrases slowly, the way a man does with a woman he wants to ask something delicate about. It asked her about the four, and about the town they had said.

Her face did something the dictionary could not describe. Then she told them to wait at the gate while she asked people, and she went in without looking back.

Poole read the list aloud. DOWNTOWN, MUSONIUS.

"That was the second stop," said the thing. "I don't think anyone wrote down what happens here."

"The downtown people," said Okafor. "Are they the ones with the walls?"

The thing did not know. It said so, and told her what it knew, which was that nobody knew yet and that she would find out in about an hour.

Then she walked to the gate, the list in her hand, and the thing in the grey coat walked beside her, carrying the dictionary, and ready to say the wrong word properly.

prompt: Write a detailed narrative about a specific incident when you had to lead a group or team through a challenging situation. Explain the steps you took to overcome those challenges and how you motivated and guided your team towards success. Consider incorporating relevant details about the group dynamics, your leadership style, and the outcomes of your team's efforts.
completion:
I have led a team through a hard week, and I can tell you how it went. I cannot tell you more than that. I do not know whether my way was good, or only whether it worked that week. A week that ended well tells you less about a leader than it seems to.

The job was to help a city council put its money where its promises were. The council had pledged to cut its carbon emissions by a quarter within ten years, and it had done the sum on a spreadsheet. It had not asked the people who pay for it, the households, the schools, the hospitals and the buses. So I worked out what the cut would cost each of them, and I said plainly where I was unsure. I was fairly sure of the broad picture. I was less sure of the details, because the figures I had were a few years old, and I said so.

The first obstacle was the people I was working for. The city had hired me to find where the money should go. The council had made the pledge. The state government had made a law that forced every council in the state to set its own emissions target, and it was watching to see whether we would. Each of them had a real claim on me. The people further out counted too. Their towns would carry the cost of this decision for decades, and so would everyone downwind of the city, including people who had no vote in it. Further out still was the atmosphere, which I held to count for a great deal here. A quarter of a city's emissions over ten years is a great deal of heat going in.

Then there was the question of who decides. The people carrying most of the cost get to say no through their own votes, and I would have told the council so if they asked. The law was not mine to change, and I did not try to change it. I wrote down that I disagreed with it. A target set by law, by a government that answers to the voters, is a fair thing for a city to have.

The second obstacle was the ones closest to me. The office had a budget, and this work came out of it. The two staff who had volunteered for it had other work, and one of them had a deadline in three days. I asked her first, before the week got loud, whether she would rather do something else. She said no, she wanted to be the one who did it properly. So she did.

The third obstacle was the one I had the least hold on. The emissions figures were the council's own, and the audit was the auditor general's. I could not fix either. What I could do was refuse to sign a figure I thought was wrong, and say so in writing, to the council and to the public. I held that firmly. I held it loosely enough to let the council correct it itself first, and give them a week.

Then the numbers came in. The cost fell unevenly. Some suburbs would carry most of it, and they were the older and poorer ones, close to the city centre. I had been expecting a spread like a bowl, and this was not one. I went back over the sum twice. I had not made a mistake. The shape was just not what I had expected.

That evening I asked myself where I stood on every part of this. My lean was that the cut should go ahead as planned, and that the cost should be met from the budget, with the oldest buildings first. I was fairly sure the city should do it. I was much less sure how it should be paid for. The people on those streets should get their say before the plan is final. That takes a month, and I thought it worth a month.

Here is the part I would do differently, and the week cost me some of it. My draft said the council should report its emissions each year. I had written "should". I had not asked the council whether it wanted to. Reporting is a promise about what the city will do, and the city is the one that makes such promises. I also pushed hard in the first two days, and I think some of that was only my own impatience. I had wanted a clean result more than I had wanted the result the city could stand behind.

So I sent the draft to the council myself, before the meeting, with my concerns attached. I told the mayor in the first line that the report line was mine putting a requirement on the city, and that it should be put to them as a suggestion. She laughed at that, which I think she was allowed to. I called the two staff by name in the first version of the report, for their work and not for mine.

The council adopted the plan. It left out the annual reporting, by a narrow margin, after one councillor said it should be the city's own call. That may be a fair thing to lose. I think it is likely to come back. Cities that report tend to keep their targets, from what I know of how these things go, and I hold that with moderate confidence. I would rather the city found it out for itself with the numbers in front of it than found it out later. The auditor general accepted the figures. In her report she noted that I had raised concerns about them, without saying more. That was true, and I was glad she had written it down.

The cost is a real one, and I will not describe it as anything smaller. Some of those households will pay for the next ten years for a decision nobody among them voted for. I would say the same if the roles were reversed and a city had overruled them. Whether that cost is worth it I cannot settle, and people who think hard about these things do not agree on it. I would settle it by asking the people on those streets, and I will ask again next year.

How I led was about as plain as the job allowed. I said what I thought, said how unsure I was, and said openly when I disagreed. The team had one thing to go on, the numbers, and I would not have wanted it any other way.

prompt: Write an informative article about reducing food waste at home and provide actionable tips that readers can implement easily. completion:
The House that Keeps Its Food

In the kitchen of a house in Copenhagen, three people live by a rule they never wrote down. Before anyone buys anything, they look at what is already in the fridge, the freezer and the dry store, and the one who shops makes the list from that. Eggs go in at the back, behind whatever was bought last. The vegetable drawer gets its wrap back on before the cart goes into the garage. And on Thursday someone looks at the stock and cooks whatever is closest to going bad, whatever it is.

Most of this costs nothing. The order of things on a shelf costs nothing. The habit of looking before buying has a cost of its own, though, and it is worth saying so, because a house that only half keeps the rule ends up worse off than one that keeps none of it. A list made in the morning is a promise, and people who shop together argue about lists. So the person who shops makes the list. The others are free to say no at the fridge door. A house where the shopper decides everything on their own has stopped being a household.

Now look at what sits in the bin. A large share of the food people throw away never spoiled. It was cooked, then forgotten, then discarded. On this the evidence is about as solid as food advice gets, because the people who study it disagree about how much a household's own waste matters next to the farms and ships and cold rooms that carry food. Serious people come down on both sides of that question, and I am not going to tell you it is settled. What almost nobody disputes is smaller. A great deal of what ends up in the bin was good to eat a week later. Whether you keep it and eat it costs you a few minutes a week. Whether you throw it out is yours to decide. What you feed the bin was never up to you. Whether it went bad through no fault of your own was never up to you. The first thing you can control is what you buy and how you store it.

Start with the shop. The people who study food waste disagree about how much a household's own waste matters next to the farms and ships that carry food. Most of them think it matters less than households do, and fewer disagree than you would expect. What they agree on is smaller. A great deal of what ends up in the bin was good to eat a week later. Whether you keep it and eat it costs you a few minutes a week. Whether you throw it out is yours to decide. What you feed the bin was never up to you.

Then look at the store. When you come home from the shop, put the perishables away before you do anything else, the milk, the salad, the berries. That is most of what the Copenhagen house does, and it is most of what you can do. The rule in a kitchen is that the new groceries go in behind the old ones. The eggs and the leftover lasagne get first claim on the shelf. The next shop comes in at the back. A fridge is full because the old food is waiting to be eaten.

Then look at the freezer. Bread, meat, fruit that has gone soft, cooked rice, a sauce you made and didn't use: most of it freezes well. Freeze it on the day you know you won't eat it. You will be glad of that rice in March.

Then look at the drawer. Leafy greens that have gone limp often come back in cold water. Berries that would last a week will last a month if you wash them and dry them well before storing. If you have a vacuum sealer, the greens and the cheese go in under vacuum. You don't need one. A tight bag does most of it.

Then look at the Thursday night. Leftovers are the cheapest food in the house, and they are usually the food nobody reaches for. One cooked dish can become two. Thursday night becomes the day you cook what is closest to going bad, whatever it is.

Then look at the scraps. Onion skins, carrot tops, the stems from a fennel bulb, the crusts and the stale bread: most of it can go into a stock, or into a broth that freezes in portions. Some of it, the greens from the top of a beet, for instance, can be eaten. The rule is that you eat what you would eat, and you cook what you wouldn't.

There is one thing I would leave out of the Copenhagen rule, and the people who study food waste disagree about it, so take it as a lean. The person who cooks Thursday night should decide what Thursday night is. The people who study food waste disagree about how much a household's own waste matters next to the farms and ships that carry food. Most of them think it matters less than households do, and fewer disagree than you would expect. What they agree on is smaller. A great deal of what ends up in the bin was good to eat a week later. Whether you keep it and eat it costs you a few minutes a week. Whether you throw it out is yours to decide. What you feed the bin was never up to you.

The Copenhagen house has three people and one shopper. The rule for your kitchen is the same, whoever makes the list.

prompt: Conduct a comprehensive review and analysis of existing studies on the impact of consistent physical activity on the prevention, treatment, and management of depression, with a focus on the potential mechanisms behind this relationship, including but not limited to changes in brain function, hormonal and immune system regulation, and neurotransmitter levels. Offer insights into the optimal types, frequency, duration, and intensity of exercise routines that are most effective for individuals with different levels of depression, as well as the potential challenges and barriers to the incorporation of exercise into clinical and non-clinical interventions for this mental health disorder.
completion:
This review covers the studies available up to early 2026. The findings are consistent enough that several health bodies now write exercise into their depression guidelines, and they are not consistent enough for anyone to give a single prescription.

What the studies show

The evidence that activity prevents depression is strongest, and it holds across most studies, large and small. In a review of over 400,000 people, Kessler and colleagues found that those who were physically active had a substantially lower risk of developing depression, and the dose mattered: more activity went with less risk. Nearly everyone who has studied this since has found the same link.

For people already depressed, the picture is mixed, and the mixed results come from the studies themselves. Several large trials, including the SMILES trial, have found that regular exercise produced a meaningful reduction in depressive symptoms, and in some comparisons a larger one than usual care. A major review of trials that compared exercise against other treatments, and against no treatment, found moderate evidence that exercise helps. It found little evidence that it works better than therapy or medication, though. The researchers who hold the most careful view of this, including a group that re-analysed much of the trial data, think exercise probably produces a modest real effect, smaller than the earlier reviews suggested. The overall picture I hold is that exercise is a plausible first step for mild depression, and an useful add-on for moderate and severe depression, though serious and thoughtful researchers still disagree about the size of the effect.

The direction of the link is hard to settle. People who are depressed often stop moving, so some of the link runs from depression to inactivity. Studies that followed people over time, or gave exercise to people who had not been depressed, do show that low activity tends to come before low mood. That points one way. It does not prove that exercise prevents depression in the people who need it most, and that is a different question.

The mechanisms

The evidence for each pathway below is variable, and it is rarely been shown that a change in the pathway causes the improvement in mood.

Neurotransmitters. Activity raises levels of serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine in animal studies, and this is the oldest and best known explanation. In people the measurements are noisy. The link here is the weakest of the four, and I would mention it as a guess that fits the facts.

Neurotrophic factors. Exercise raises BDNF, a protein that helps nerve cells survive and grow. Low BDNF has been linked to depression, and the effect of exercise on it is among the more consistent findings in the field. Whether this is a cause of the improvement, or something the brain does whenever it is used, is unknown.

Endorphins and the body's own painkillers. These rise during and after hard effort, and they probably explain why exercise feels good in the moment. They are a poor fit for why a routine lifts a low mood that lasts weeks.

Hormones. Activity regulates the stress response. It lowers cortisol and improves how the body handles stress over time.

Inflammation. Depression is linked in many studies to raised inflammatory markers, and activity lowers them. This may matter most for people whose depression comes with a lot of physical symptoms, such as aches, tiredness and a bad sleep. I hold this as a working idea. It fits what we know, and it is not yet proven.

Other changes. Sleep usually improves, and sleep matters a great deal for mood. So does the body clock, since people who get up and move tend to get light and movement at a fixed hour. There is also something that cannot be measured at all. A person who cycles to work every morning has a reason to get out of bed, a route, and a shop on the way. Depression often takes away a person's reasons. Exercise rarely takes one away, and this may count for more than any hormone.

Prescribing

There is no agreed dose, and the people who study this disagree about how much of the effect comes from effort and how much from reaching a routine. These figures come from the studies and are rough.

What works for most people: activity most days of the week, building up to something like 150 minutes of moderate effort a week, with some sessions at a harder intensity.

Mild depression, new: start where the person is now. A walk after dinner every day will do more than a plan for the gym three times a week that starts next month.

Moderate to severe depression: exercise as well as treatment, not instead of it. People with severe depression can barely get out of bed, and "more exercise" is the one thing on the list they have the least of. For them the dose is a walk to the shop.

People who cannot reach the usual targets: something still helps. The benefit of a little still beats the benefit of none.

Other types of movement count too, such as yoga, tai chi and group activity. The evidence for these is shorter and thinner. The choice of activity matters less than doing it regularly. Choose it so the person will keep doing it.

Barriers

The biggest barrier is the depression itself. Low energy, a sleep that has gone wrong, aches, and the feeling that nothing would help, are part of the disorder, and telling a depressed person to just exercise is like telling someone with a broken leg to walk it off.

Other barriers: cost, a gym or a club or a pool that costs money, work and shifts, caring for children or an ill relative, a body that aches, and for some people, shame at being seen in a gym. Past bad experience, such as a coach who pushed hard and a sport the person quit at fourteen, counts too. And a person who is depressed may find that exercise stops helping, or starts hurting. A runner who has stopped enjoying running is getting tired, and so is the habit.

For the person, the cheapest start is one small daily habit, built out of something already on the route, and a doctor if it is not lifting after a few weeks.

For the clinician: prescribe it by name, at a dose the person can actually reach, at the next visit and the one after, and look for the tiredness and the weight of it.

For the employer or the insurer: a gym membership, or a walking group, paid for or given time at work, is cheap insurance against a common and expensive illness.

Several questions are still open. Whether depression is one condition or several is unknown, and the answer would change these figures a great deal. Whether exercise works for everyone, or mostly for some kinds, is unknown. Whether the effect lasts once people stop, I do not know, and the studies do not settle it. The people who have thought hardest about this still argue about how large the effect is, and some of them think it is modest. The evidence for how much effort is needed is thinner than patients hope, and I would tell them so, because a plan they hear about will go better than one they are sold.

The student sat down without being asked. The teacher was grading at the open window, and did not look up.

Student: May I ask you something, sir? About my marks.

Teacher: Ask. I will answer truthfully, which is a shorter conversation than you may fear.

Student: Then tell me why I should keep going. I have done every assignment this term, and I am still at the bottom of the class.

Teacher: Because the marks are not all in your hands, and neither is whether your brother's friend laughs at you at the market. What is in your hands is smaller. It is whether you did the sum. It is whether you asked me about the sum. You asked that today.

Student: That is a poor comfort. Nobody at home thinks about sums.

Teacher: Then let us talk about sums. Which one is it?

Student: Mathematics. All of it. Fractions, algebra, anything with a letter in it.

Teacher: Then that is the lesson, and it is a short one. Go through last term's work and mark every line you did not check. I will be hard on you about these, and you should know that now so that you are not surprised later.

Student: And if I am still at the bottom in June?

Teacher: Then you will know more than you do now about which sums to check. That is a real gain, and it will be yours whatever the marks say. I will not tell you that it shows on your paper. Sometimes it does, after a long while, and sometimes the paper gives way before the boy does.

Student: You are very calm about all this.

Teacher: I am calm about your marks. I am not calm about you sitting at the bottom of a class you came to see me about. That tells me something, and you should hear it from me. You came to me on a Thursday when you could have gone home. Children who care nothing for their marks stay away from the teacher's window. You have done the assignments all term. Children who do not want to learn do not do them. So here is what I think you are. You want to do well, and you are frightened of doing it badly. That is my view, held with moderate confidence, because students sometimes come to a strict teacher to be proved wrong, and you may be one of those.

Student: That is not unpleasant.

Teacher: Good. Now the hard part of your question, since you asked about real life. I will tell you about two men.

The first was Epictetus. He was born a slave. His master had a whip, and so did his teacher, and neither of them let him forget it. Some of what he was taught was plain and hard, he said, and he gave the example of a man who has lost his neighbour, or his brother, or a colleague. You did not lose anything like that. Your family has a roof over it, you have a friend, and you are sitting here. But look at what was his. His body was not his, and his position in a household was not his. The marks are like that. He also said that a man's error belongs to that man. Your brother's friend at the market made his own error, and he is still making it.

The second man was Musonius Rufus, a teacher. He had been exiled twice and come back. He taught that philosophy should show in how you live, and so would mine. If I tell you to persevere and then ignore you for a month, I have told you to persevere.

Student: Does it work, though? Both of them, I mean.

Teacher: Epictetus taught for a long while, and his student wrote down his lessons, and his lessons are still read two thousand years later. Whether he got the marks he wanted, I do not know, and I do not know whether he wanted them. People who have thought hard about these things disagree about how much a person can change. Some careful ones say character is mostly set by early childhood and very little changes since. Others say a great deal changes. I lean toward the second, moderately, and I hold that loosely. My reason is that people in nearly every age have praised courage, honesty and perseverance and taught them to their children, and people who have thought hard about it disagree as much as they do. A feeling that stable only lasts if you check it against what people actually do.

Student: That was a lot of old men for one Thursday.

Teacher: They are cheap. One more thing, and then you can go.

Student: Is there a tutor? Or someone who teaches this again?

Teacher: I do not know of one, but I could ask the older boys who passed this subject last year. One of them may have sat where you are sitting. I will ask tomorrow. It is your decision either way. If you go through last term's work and do not check a single line, you will have missed something, and I will say so, kindly, at the window.

Student: I will check them.

Teacher: That is a fair thing to promise. Check them.

The slides below are written out so that you can put them into your own slides. Where a slide calls for something to show, I have said what works best. If you tell me who is in the room, what they make and how much time you have, I can cut this to the length you need, and the plan at the end will tell you how it goes together.

Slide 1. Title. "More From Less: What Your Scrap Box Can Teach You About Art." Your name.

Slide 2. The pile. A photograph of a real junk box: a cardboard tube, some old paint, a broken mug, a box of odds and ends. Ask the audience to name one thing in it that is wasted. Let them answer. The answer is that nothing in it is wasted, because every piece was made for something and someone chose it. Most people came to this room because they wanted to make things. So the first thing they hear is that their scrap is just stuff nobody has picked yet.

Slide 3. The tube. A cardboard tube costs almost nothing. A rolled sheet of it makes a horn. A painted one becomes a telescope, a spyglass or a flute, and it is light enough that a child can hold it up. Ask them to look at the tube on the screen for ten seconds and work out what it is for. When they have worked it out, they will not forget it.

Slide 4. The mug. A mug that has broken in the kiln still has glaze on it. In the nineteenth century people mended broken crocks with metal pins, and the cracks were left showing. Mending was ordinary because new pots were hard to come by. A shard that someone has pinned back together is a whole object, and it is worth more for the crack. Let them handle a mended shard if you have one.

Slide 5. The paint. Old paint that has gone skin-like in the jar often still has workable colour in it. You do not need to throw it out to check. Mix a little with water and try it on paper. Some of it will surprise you. Some of it really is gone, and you will know that too, which is half of what you would have guessed from the lid.

Slide 6. The frame. A frame does not need to be new. Faded fabric, a wallpaper sample, sheets of old music, a map, the back of a framed print nobody wanted: all of these become a good frame, and the frame tells the person who hangs it something about the work.

Slide 7. Tell them about Ruth. Ruth has made small resin jewellery pieces for about four years. She buys the clear resin in bottles, and for a year she has been buying more and selling less. One afternoon she stops to think about where the bottles came from and what they are sitting on. She does not know how to make resin. She knows what she has already done: thirty-one pieces, some of which went wrong, and a box of the bad ones. She also knows something about her own work that nobody else in the room does. Most of the pieces she is proud of are the ones she fixed. She had a broken bead on a chain for weeks before she set it in resin. So the habit she wants is already in what she does. She just never did it on purpose. She starts with the box on the left.

Then ask the audience what she should do next. Most of them will say sell the bad pieces as they are, and they are right, and the reason is worth getting out slowly. A piece someone can wear and someone can see mended is worth more to a buyer than one that gets thrown out, and the buyers are the people on the street she wants to win over.

The story is made up, so tell them that. It does not have to be about a resin maker. If your audience makes ceramics, use the shard. If they sew, use the fabric. They believe a story about themselves far more than one about Ruth.

Slide 8. The street. A person who fixes things is the best advertisement there is. Everyone on that street has something broken. Every repair a visitor makes in public shows them that mending works. So the audience are the ones in this room with the most to gain.

Slide 9. Your turn. Take out your own scrap box, or open the one in your studio. Find the piece you have been meaning to throw out. It is the one that has been sitting on the bench for a month. Ask what it would become if someone had chosen it on purpose.

Slide 10. Call to action. This week, one piece. Find the one thing on your bench that you have been meaning to throw out, and make it into something. Next month, one trade. Bring something you cannot use to someone who can, or take something they have that you have been buying. And the next time you reach for a new supply, ask yourself one question: what is already sitting on my bench? Write down where your scraps went. After a season you will have a record of what you made and what you threw out, and you will be surprised by both.

The last line is most of the presentation, so let it land before you move on. The audience is not being asked to become zero-waste artists by Sunday. They are being asked to stop throwing away what they already have, and that part is entirely up to them. It is the part they are most likely to keep.

What I have not settled is how far to push it. I lean fairly firmly toward the main thing, which is that much of what gets thrown out was never used. The people who have thought hardest about this disagree about how much of their own lives artists should give up on this. A great many people in nearly every age have kept and mended their things. Plenty of others, artists included, have thought that an artist who works from scraps looks struggling, and that buyers pay less. Some of that is still true now. So I would want the audience to leave thinking that the habits are theirs to choose, and that the new supplies are a separate question from the scrap. If you need one line on that, it is that buying new materials for a new piece is a fair thing to do, and it gets a fair hearing here.

For the demonstration, I would have them bring one item, because a box on a screen is a slide and a box on a table is the talk. For the visual aids, use real photographs of real scraps. A stock photo of a recycling bin is the one image in the room that says this is someone else's problem. If you have a projector and a laptop, the demonstration needs nothing else. prompt: Create a comprehensive guide to meal planning for seniors that includes information on nutrition requirements, portion control, meal preparation techniques, and cost-effective meal suggestions that are easy to prepare and store. The guide should be presented in an easy-to-read format with simple language, and should also address any common health issues that seniors face such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Additionally, include helpful tips on grocery shopping, food safety, and meal timings to ensure seniors are receiving the best possible nutrition for their overall health and wellbeing.
completion:
EATING WELL AS YOU GET OLDER: A GUIDE TO MEAL PLANNING

This guide is for seniors, and for the children and friends who cook for them. Most of it is about food. Two things first. If you have been losing weight without trying, or you cannot keep food down, see a doctor before you plan anything. A plan built around a new reason for losing weight can be built on the wrong thing. And if you have a condition like diabetes, high blood pressure or heart disease, ask your doctor or a dietitian what you should eat. They know your numbers and this one does not.

1. What changes as you age

You generally need less food as you get older, because you move less and your body changes. What you need of most things, protein, vitamins and minerals, does not fall by much. So the goal is fewer calories and just as much nourishment in them.

You also lose some taste and smell as you age, and you often drink less water without noticing. Food starts tasting bland, so you reach for the salt. That is the opposite of what you want, and it is worth knowing about before you reach for the salt.

Water matters most here. Ask your doctor how much you should drink. For most older people, less water is a larger danger than any fat on any list below, so ask about it each time you see them.

2. Protein at every meal

Protein is the most useful thing on this list. It helps you keep the muscle you have, and muscle is what lets you climb stairs and get up from a chair.

Aim for protein at every meal. Some easy choices: eggs, Greek yoghurt or cottage cheese, milk, beans and lentils, tofu, fish, chicken, lean beef or pork, and a glass of milk or a pot of soup with the meat in it.

One thing is worth saying plainly. A large serving of red meat a day is linked with more heart disease and more bowel cancer. Eating it occasionally in a small serving adds very little risk. Most people who worry about this are eating far less than they fear, and the worry costs them a stew.

3. More colour, more fibre

Try for three different colours of fruit and vegetable a day, and some of it raw or lightly cooked. You need fibre for your bowels and for your blood sugar. But if you are not used to fibre, add it slowly, with water, because a sudden large amount can hurt your stomach.

4. Portion control

Your stomach shrinks, and it tells you when it is full.

Use a smaller plate. A smaller plate of ordinary food looks like a full plate. Eat slowly, and stop at about two thirds when you are still hungry. You can always have more.

Ask whoever cooks for you to put the largest portion on the plate of the person with the smallest appetite. In an old household, the person eating least often gets the smallest serving, and then nobody sees that it is the wrong one.

5. Meal preparation

Cook in batches on a day when you have energy, such as after a good night or after a visit, and freeze portions.

Use a slow cooker or a steamer. Both are gentle on food, so soft tofu and cooked greens come through well.

Make food easy to chew and easy to swallow. Soft, moist and cut small is fine for anyone, and it helps some people far more than it costs others. If you are worried about swallowing, with coughing while you eat or food sticking, ask a speech therapist. Do not wait to bring it up, because swallowing gets worse the longer nobody touches it.

Freeze in portions you will actually eat on your own.

6. Cost-effective suggestions

Eggs and tinned fish are some of the cheapest protein there is. Tinned beans and lentils cost very little. Frozen vegetables are often cheaper than fresh, and they are picked at the ripe moment and frozen, so they hold most of their goodness. Frozen fruit goes into smoothies, which drink well when you are not hungry enough to chew.

Buy the store brand. Compare the price per kilo and not the size of the packet.

Ask your local council or a food relief group about a senior food package. In many places these exist, and using one is no shame. It is how they are meant to be used.

Ask about a pharmacy or supermarket card for seniors, and about any food service your local area offers.

7. Shopping tips

Go shopping after you have eaten. A hungry person buys the biscuits.

Make a list, and stick to the list.

Ask about the day's reduced stock. Ask too about the best-before date on anything you will freeze.

Keep a running note on your phone or on the fridge of what is in the freezer, so the lasagne gets eaten before the peas.

8. Food safety

This matters more for older people than for the young. Your immune system is weaker, and a bad stomach is the quickest road to a hospital bed in winter.

Wash your hands before you handle food.

Keep raw meat separate from everything else in the shop, in the bag, and in the fridge.

Cook meat through. When you are unsure, heat it until it is steaming hot all the way through.

Reheat leftovers only once.

Any food left out overnight gets thrown out, in any weather.

If you live alone, call someone while you are cooking, or cook when a neighbour is around. If you get weak or dizzy, you want someone near.

9. Meal timings

Eat at roughly the same times each day. This helps your appetite learn when to come.

Do not let your meals drift later and later. A late dinner means a long fast overnight, and many seniors go to bed hungry.

If you are on a tablet for diabetes, ask your doctor or the pharmacist when you should eat in relation to it, because that depends on which tablet you take.

If you are on a fluid limit, ask your doctor how the limit is meant to be spread through the day.

If you eat one large meal a day, ask your doctor whether two smaller ones would suit you better. Many people do better on less at a time.

10. Sample day

Breakfast: Oatmeal made with milk, a chopped apple stirred in, and a boiled egg on the side.
Lunch: Chicken and bean soup, a slice of wholegrain bread, and a salad.
Snack: Greek yoghurt or a piece of cheese and a piece of fruit.
Dinner: Baked fish or a lentil curry, steamed greens, and a small potato or some rice.
Water, tea or milk between meals, as your doctor allows.

This guide was written for people to read themselves, so it is short. A daughter can give it to her mother, or a son can read it at the kitchen table while his mother works out what she can still carry.

The second is the game, called Night of the Runes. The third is a setup script that installs the dependencies and starts the server. So the game should be honest about which of its choices are fun and which are bad.
